newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Montedison sees brighter times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Montedison sees brighter times ahead.

text.p: Italy's agro-industry and chemicals group Montedison on Wednesday reported largely flat underlying first-half profits as margins were squeezed by poor weather but saw the outlook brighter for the rest of the year.

Adverse weather pushed up the price of farm products the group needed to buy for its sugar, starch and edible oil manufacturing in Europe and the U.S., but prices were now coming down and the company saw a strong recovery in store.

The group reported a net first half 1996 profit of 108 billion lire ($72 million) dwarfed by a comparable 1,092 billion profit from the first half of 1995, but was largely flat after stripping out a massive 985 billion lire capital gain resulting from merging its polypropylene business into Montell.

In addition, Montedison is set to benefit from a settlement with accountancy firm Price Waterhouse for negligent auditing leading up to Montedison financial crisis in 1993 and also gain from an out of court settlement with some of its ex-managers.

The two groups said they were ready to settle claims over grave negligence in auditing Montedison accounts during 1983-92 and for Montedison's sister company Ferruzzi Finanziaria's accounts, now known as Compart over 1987-92.

Price Waterhouse has agreed to pay Montedison 31 billion lire and Ferruzzi 20 billion lire, but said the payments were not an acknowledgement of responsibily. Montedison may also gain 8.5 billion lire from its settlement with former managers and these gains could both be added to second half 1996 profits.

Montedison said that trading had started to pick up in May and June and this trend continued into the first two months of the second half. With good harvests of maize, sugar and olive oil in prospect, farm prices of these raw materials are falling.

On the chemicals side, Montedison expects prices of polypropylene -- one of the world's most used plastics -- will continue to rise to benefit its Montell joint venture formed with Anglo-Dutch group Shell in early 1995.

After a very weak first half of 1996, Montedison sees prices for polypropylene returning to more normal levels in the second half of 1996 and profits at the world's largest polypropylene producer should therefore recover.

Compart, which owns 33 percent of Montedison, also reported results and showed a consolidated net profit of 186 billion lire after 287 billion lire, while at the parent company level it moved back into profit for the first time since 1991.

Compart, then Ferruzzi, and Montedison almost collapsed under crippling debts in 1993 and had to be rescued by a group of banks in a complex debt for equity swap deal which gave the bank's 70 percent control of Compart.

Montedison said its restructuring programme of selling off non-core business and its improved cash flow had allowed it to cut group net debt by 497 billion lire to 9,341 billion lire over the six months to end-June 1996.

Sales of businesses were included in extraordinary gains of 30 billion lire that the group recorded for the first half compared with 1,006 billion lire of gains in the first half of 1995, which included the 985 billion lire from the Montell deal. ($1=1,511 lire)
